title: What is the education data spine?
subject: The Data Spine
statusStamp: DFE · ANNOUNCED FEB 2026 · NOT YET BUILT
thesis: In February 2026 the government committed, in one paragraph of a white paper, to build a “data spine” for English education. This project takes that paragraph seriously — what a spine is, what it would be worth, who wants what from it, and how it could be built without repeating the mistakes already made with children's data.

status.headline: Announced, unspecified, unbuilt.
status.detail: Consultation promised for summer 2026; the white paper's own phasing puts implementation at 2028–29.

findings.text: The public specification of the spine fits in three quotations. Everything that matters — custody, architecture, who may look — is undecided.
The long tail of suppliers, not the three majors, is the binding design constraint — and it serves nurseries, special schools and alternative provision.
A federated spine can answer the department's questions without a new central store. The remaining obstacle is legal and political, not technical.

asks: What exactly has been announced — and what remains undecided?
What is a data spine made of, and what are the options at each layer?
How does it differ from the consistent child identifier, and why does confusing them matter?
Could it be built without spending the last of the public's trust?

beats.name: The problem
beats.question: What exactly has been announced, and by whom?

claim.text: The entire public record of the spine is three quotations. Everything a design would need is still to be decided.

prose.research: The full public specification of the data spine fits in three quotations. The white paper names the data in scope and the qualities demanded — and nothing else: no architecture, no custodian, no budget, no delivery date.
prose.plain: Three quotes are the entire public record. Everything else is still to be decided.

beats.pullQuote: One paragraph, on page 98, with no architecture attached.

sections.title: How England got here

threads.name: Capability built
threads.detail: NPD, the attendance feed, the Education Record, now the spine. Each one made the next possible.

threads.name: Trust spent
threads.detail: ContactPoint, the distribution era, the Home Office MoU, the ICO audit. Each one made the next harder.

entries.title: The National Pupil Database begins
entries.detail: Census returns become a permanent longitudinal record. No sunset clause was ever set.

entries.title: ContactPoint is switched off
entries.detail: A national index of every child, cancelled on cost and proportionality. The objections were never answered.

entries.title: The Home Office memorandum
entries.detail: School census data shared for immigration enforcement.

entries.title: The ICO audit
entries.detail: The regulator found the department in breach of data-protection law.

entries.title: Daily attendance goes mandatory
entries.detail: Automated extraction from every state school's MIS — the spine's proof of concept, under a commercial contract.

entries.title: Data (Use and Access) Act
entries.detail: The legal plumbing a spine would run on, plus the consistent child identifier in statute.

entries.title: The white paper commits to a spine
entries.detail: One paragraph on page 98. Consultation promised for the summer.

sections.balance: The two accounts do not net off. Capability compounds while trust depletes, and the consultation inherits the balance of both.

beats.soWhat: There is less here than the debate assumes. The argument is not about a system that exists — it is about a paragraph.

openQuestion.text: Has the trust account ever recovered anywhere, after a breach of this kind?

beats.name: The estate & the evidence
beats.question: What exists today, who holds it, and how do we know?

claim.text: Three suppliers cover four schools in five — but the twelve that cover the rest are the ones serving nurseries, special schools and alternative provision.

beats.standfirst: Nobody can design a spine without knowing how many estates it has to reach. So: every supplier, with a real number against it, and the date the number was true.

survey.provenance: WhichMIS, October 2025. Every count reconciles to the 22,018 state census; the estimate band is excluded from that total and from every share.
cannotTellYou: How many children appear in more than one estate under different identifiers.
Whether the long tail could afford a query interface at all.
Anything about independent schools or early years, which are not in the census.

sections.title: It has been tried before

claim.text: Every spine that died was a central store; every one that survived moved questions. The sample is small, but unanimous.

cases.name: NHS Spine
cases.what: Demographics service plus a record locator. Holds identity and pointers; records stay in trusts.
cases.lesson: The name everyone borrows was never a database.

cases.name: X-Road
cases.what: A query fabric across the whole state. No central copy; every request logged and citizen-visible.
cases.lesson: Citizens tolerate the plumbing because they can watch it.

cases.name: ContactPoint
cases.what: An index of all 11 million children, with 390,000 authorised users.
cases.lesson: Scale of access, not scale of data, is what ended it.

cases.name: CPR
cases.what: A civil registration number used across every public service, with statutory purpose limits.
cases.lesson: An identifier is survivable if the limits arrive with it.

pattern: Survivors hold identity and audit centrally, and nothing else. The three that died all held records.
Survivors made access visible to the citizen from the start. Retrofitting transparency has never once worked.
Every failure was political, not technical. All three cancelled systems worked as specified when switched off.

beats.soWhat: The estate is more concentrated than the debate assumes and more fragmented than a designer would like. Both facts constrain the answer, and they pull in opposite directions.

openQuestion.text: Nobody publishes how many of the 22,018 could serve a query today. The department must know; it has not said.

beats.name: Ways to build it
beats.question: If you had to build it, what are the actual options — and which have already been tried?

claim.text: There are four archetypes, not a spectrum — three have a real precedent, and only one requires copying children's records into a new store.

marginNotes.text: The word does five jobs. Collapsing them into “database” is how the argument gets lost.

prose.research: Every school already keeps its register in a management information system. The question the consultation must answer is custody: connect those estates with a query fabric, or collect them into another central store.
prose.plain: Schools already hold the data. The question is whether the government asks them, or copies it.

prose.research: Where a spine has succeeded, the pattern is consistent. The centre holds identity, permission and audit. The records stay where they are generated.

figures.caption: The four archetypes and their fates. Three are already running in British government; the accent marks the one this study goes on to defend in beat 04.
A schools × local-authority join, modelled. The dropped column is the one that matters: those children exist, and the answer silently excludes them.

beats.pullQuote: The department does not need to invent an architecture. It needs to choose one and say so.

claim.text: Four of the five layers already exist in some form. The one that does not — governance — is the one every objection is actually about.

layers.name: Identifier
layers.question: who is this child?
layers.today: UPN in schools, ULN post-16, NHS number in health. None reconcile.
layers.withIt: One consistent identifier, in statute, with pilots running.
layers.theFight: Whether it becomes a de facto national ID.

layers.name: Index
layers.question: who holds a record?
layers.today: Nothing. Finding a child's history means asking around.
layers.withIt: A record-locator registry: pointers only, no content.
layers.theFight: A pointer index is itself sensitive — it maps a life.

layers.name: Exchange
layers.question: how does it move?
layers.today: A rented commercial pipe, plus 2,385 bespoke distributions.
layers.withIt: A query fabric the department governs itself.
layers.theFight: Connect or collect. This is the whole argument.

layers.name: Standards
layers.question: do we mean the same thing?
layers.today: Census specifications, revised annually, interpreted locally.
layers.withIt: A published semantic layer — and a resolution standard.
layers.theFight: The resolution standard does not exist. Nothing works without it.

layers.name: Governance
layers.question: who may ask, and who checks?
layers.today: Policy, not statute. An ICO audit found the law was broken.
layers.withIt: Purpose limits in law, an append-only audit ledger, a public dashboard.
layers.theFight: Entirely undesigned — and the subject of beat 06.

beats.soWhat: Three of the four archetypes are already running somewhere in British government. The choice is available; what is missing is a decision, and the standard that makes it work.

openQuestion.text: No lawful shared analytic key exists across schools, local authorities and health. Every join in this study is therefore probabilistic.

beats.name: The recommendation
beats.question: Which archetype, and why that one?

position.statement: Centralise the trust, not the data.
position.elaboration: Build the identity, permission and audit layers nationally, once, and govern them in public. Leave every pupil record in the estate that generates it. Move questions, not children.

because.headline: It is the only archetype with a working precedent at national scale.
because.detail: X-Road has run for 24 years across a whole government; the NHS Spine for twenty.

because.headline: It answers the stated questions without a new copy to defend.
because.detail: Every question in the white paper is an aggregate. None needs the records in one place.

because.headline: It is the only design where an opt-out still means something.
because.detail: A record never copied can still be withheld. A record already in a warehouse cannot.

rejected.name: Central store
rejected.why: Cancelled once already, on precisely these objections, and nothing about them has changed except the public's patience.

rejected.name: Broker pipe
rejected.why: It works today — that is the strongest argument for it. But the department rents the governance rather than holding it, and cannot show a parent the audit trail of a system it does not run.

rejected.name: Index & locate
rejected.why: Sound, cheap, and insufficient. A pointer registry can tell you who holds a record; it cannot answer how many children in a local authority were absent last week.

conditions: Statutory purpose limits, not policy ones
A transparency dashboard live from the first query
Funding for the long tail's query interface
position.sinkers: If the long tail cannot be brought to a query interface at acceptable cost, federation degrades into a broker pipe with extra steps — and the department will have spent the trust for nothing.

phases.label: Phase 1
phases.name: The standard
phases.detail: Publish identity resolution. Nothing works without it.

phases.label: Phase 2
phases.name: The audit ledger
phases.detail: Before any query runs, so the first one is on the record.

phases.label: Phase 3
phases.name: Three estates
phases.detail: The majors, one question, in public. Then measure.

phases.label: Phase 4
phases.name: The long tail
phases.detail: Funded, not mandated. This is where it succeeds or fails.

beats.soWhat: This is a recommendation the department could adopt in the consultation without new legislation. The expensive part is not the technology — it is publishing a standard and then living by it.

openQuestion.text: Is there any lawful route to a shared analytic key across schools, local authorities and health?
openQuestion.falsifier: a DUAA route nobody has used yet

beats.name: What it does & who wins
beats.question: Who is better off if this is built, and who is worse off?

claim.text: Nineteen entries, and the ledger is close to even — because almost every benefit depends on the department also doing something it has not committed to.

benefits.text: A child moving school keeps their record

risks.text: An opt-out that cannot be honoured
Small suppliers priced out of compliance

ledger.balance: Read as a parent, the ledger tips negative — not because the benefits are small, but because every one of them is conditional and every risk is structural.

byActor.quote: Show me the audit trail first.
Stop asking us for the same return twice.

beats.soWhat: The winners are institutional and the losers are individual, which is the shape of every data programme that has failed politically.

openQuestion.text: Nobody has asked parents what they would trade. Every entry on their side of this page is inferred.

beats.name: Trust & safeguards
beats.question: What could go wrong, and what would actually stop it?

claim.text: Every safeguard proposed so far is policy, not law — and policy is what failed the last four times.

benefits.text: Query-not-copy is auditable in a way bulk distribution never was
DUAA 2025 provides a lawful basis that does not need new primary legislation

risks.text: The 2016 Home Office memorandum has no statutory bar on repetition
2,385 NPD distributions remain outside any single audit trail
Purpose limits held in policy can be changed without Parliament

ledger.balance: The architecture can be made trustworthy. The governance, as announced, cannot — because nothing in it is binding on a future minister.

beats.soWhat: Architecture alone cannot answer the objections. The safeguards have to be the kind that survive a change of government.

openQuestion.text: Would statutory purpose limits actually pass, given the Home Office's interest in the same data?

beats.name: What happens next
beats.question: What would change the picture, and when?

claim.text: Three things are due before the end of 2026, and one of them decides everything else.

position.statement: Watch the consultation for one word: custody.
position.elaboration: The consultation document will either name an architecture or defer it. If it defers, the broker pipe becomes the spine by default — not by decision.

because.headline: Summer 2026: the consultation opens.
because.detail: The first document that could contain an architecture.

because.headline: 2028–29: the white paper's own implementation window.
Meanwhile the attendance feed keeps running.
because.detail: Every month it runs, the default hardens.

rejected.name: Waiting for the consultation to ask better questions
rejected.why: Consultations answer the questions they are given. The architecture question has to be raised before the document is drafted, not after.

position.sinkers: Deferral. A consultation that does not name a custody model has already chosen the incumbent.

phases.label: Open
phases.name: The resolution standard
phases.detail: Still unwritten. The single largest gap in this study.

phases.label: Open
phases.name: The custodian
phases.detail: No named owner for any layer.

beats.soWhat: The decision that matters will be made by whether the consultation document uses the word custody — and it may be made by not using it.

openQuestion.text: Is the consultation drafted already? If so, none of this analysis reaches it in time.
